chunks: I2C versus SPI differences. The question: What is the difference between I2C and SPI?
I2C and SPI both move bytes between a main chip (the controller) and helper chips, using a shared clock. They differ in how a device is picked and how wires are driven.
SPI gives each device its own select wire and drives every wire hard, so it is fast but uses more pins.
I2C puts the device's address on the data wire and lets a resistor pull the wires high, so it uses two wires but is slower.
In a room of people, SPI is tapping one person on the shoulder and then speaking quickly. It is fast, but each person needs their own tap, and an empty chair never answers.
I2C is calling out a name to the whole room and waiting for that person to say "yes." It is slower, but needs no private line, and silence means the person is missing.
SPI's pin count grows linearly with the number of targets while I2C stays flat.
Daisy-chaining (for parts that support it) flattens SPI too, but the whole chain is read or written as one long shift register. See "SPI daisy-chaining explained".
Chip select: a dedicated wire that wakes up one SPI device. Address: a number sent on the shared wires that picks one I2C device ("I2C, SPI and UART: how each works").
ACK: the receiver's reply bit meaning "I got that." SPI has none. Pull-up resistor: a resistor that lifts an I2C wire to high when no device pulls it low.
It makes the climb from low to high slow. Full duplex: data flowing both ways at once, as in SPI.
On I2C at 400 kilohertz, it is 14 data bytes plus 3 overhead bytes (the address, the register number, the address again; a register is a numbered slot), at 9 clock ticks each.
So 17 times 9 = 153 ticks, about 382 microseconds. On SPI at 10 megahertz, it is 1 command byte plus 14 data bytes at 8 ticks each, 120 ticks, or 12 microseconds.
That is about 30 times faster, at the cost of a select wire per device. That is the whole idea.
"SPI is four-plus wires, push-pull, full duplex and fast, but every extra device costs a chip-select pin.
I2C is two shared open-drain wires with pull-ups, devices selected by address, half duplex and slower, but it adds ACK, multi-master and clock stretching.
So I2C scales better in pins, SPI scales better in speed. I'd use I2C for many slow sensors and SPI for flash, displays, or high-rate ADCs."
